posts.quote: A LONG-DISTANCE CALL WAS TIMED BY THE KITCHEN CLOCK, AND EVERYBODY TALKED FAST.
posts.caption: When Aunt Ruth called from Ohio, the whole house went quiet. Mom stood by the wall phone with one eye on the kitchen clock and the other on the cord. Long distance was charged by the minute, so the news came in a rush: who was sick, who was married, who had finally sold the truck. Nobody said how are you twice. At the three-minute mark Mom would say well, I'd better let you go, and she meant every word of it. Then she hung up and told us everything all over again, slowly, over supper.
posts.first: Our call from my grandmother in Tennessee always came on Sunday after the rates dropped. She fit her whole week into about ninety seconds and then asked to hear the dog bark. I never did figure out how she managed it.

posts.quote: THE LUNCH BAG HAD YOUR NAME ON IT IN MARKER, AND IT LASTED THE WHOLE SCHOOL YEAR.
posts.caption: Every morning a brown paper bag sat on the kitchen counter with your name across it in thick black marker. Inside was a sandwich folded in waxed paper, an apple, and maybe a cookie if the week had gone well. You carried that bag to school, ate your lunch, and folded the bag back flat. It rode home in your pocket and came back out the next morning. By spring it was soft as cloth and had been through more cafeterias than the principal. Nobody bought a new one until it finally tore.
posts.first: Mine was folded so many times it had a crease down the middle like a map. My mother wrote my name the same way every day, block letters, same marker. I would know that handwriting anywhere.

posts.quote: Every family had a drawer with a key nobody could identify and nobody was willing to throw away.
posts.first: There was a small brass one in ours. Dad swore it fit something in the old house. We left that house forty years ago, and the key came along.

posts.character: Thrift and winter (the bread bag boots)
posts.quote: A BREAD BAG OVER YOUR SOCK KEPT THE SNOW OUT OF YOUR BOOT, AND NOBODY THOUGHT IT STRANGE.
posts.caption: Snow boots back then were rubber, and rubber leaked. So before you went out, Mom slid a bread bag over each sock and tucked the twist tie at your ankle. It crackled when you walked. Your feet stayed dry, and you could stay out in the drifts until your fingers quit working. Nobody called it a trick. It was just what you did with a bread bag once the bread was gone. Mom kept a drawer of them for exactly that reason.
posts.first: I wore bread bags in my boots all through the winter of 1962. The crackle gave me away every time I tried to sneak up on my brother. I would still take it over any pair of wool socks.

posts.quote: THE MEDICINE CABINET / A BOTTLE OF RED ANTISEPTIC, A TIN OF BANDAGES, AND A KISS ON THE KNEE
posts.caption: You came in through the screen door with a scraped knee and a brave face that lasted exactly as long as it took to see the bottle. Mom sat you on the edge of the tub and dabbed on that bright orange-red liquid, which stung and stained and meant business. Then came the bandage from the little tin, and a kiss right on top of it. You were told to quit crying, and you did. The stain stayed on your knee for a week like a medal. By Saturday you had earned a new one.
posts.first: Our cabinet had a mirror on the door that squeaked when it opened. Everything inside smelled like a doctor's office, only friendlier. I can still feel the cold tile under my feet when I think about it.

posts.quote: THE CHRISTMAS LIGHTS WENT BACK IN THE BOX IN ONE KNOT AND CAME OUT IN DECEMBER IN A BIGGER ONE.
posts.caption: Every January Dad swore he would wrap the Christmas lights neatly around a piece of cardboard. Every January he dumped them in the box in a heap and shoved the lid down. Come December he sat on the living room floor with a ball of green wire in his lap and the face of a man defusing something. We kids sat nearby, offering advice he never asked for. An hour later it was untangled, and exactly one bulb on the whole string wouldn't light. He tested every bulb until he found it, and he never said a word about next year.
posts.first: Our string had a bulb at the very end that stayed dark for as long as I can remember. Dad would take it out, look at it like it owed him money, and screw it back in. It never lit and it never got thrown away.

posts.quote: THE DENTIST'S WAITING ROOM HAD A FISH TANK, A STACK OF OLD MAGAZINES, AND NO WAY TO FEEL BETTER.
posts.caption: The dentist's waiting room had green vinyl chairs and one fish tank bubbling in the corner. You watched the same fish circle the same plastic castle while your stomach did laps of its own. The magazines on the table were two years old and had half the pages folded down. Someone had already done the crossword in pen. A door opened, a nurse called a name, and every kid in the room stared at the floor. It wasn't yours, and it felt like winning a prize.
posts.first: Our dentist kept a bowl of cheap toy rings at the front desk for brave patients. I took one every visit, whether I earned it or not. I think he knew.

posts.character: Family life (carried in from the car)
posts.quote: The best part of a long drive home was falling asleep in the back seat and being carried inside without waking.
posts.first: My dad carried me in that way until I was well past too old for it. I always knew exactly what he was doing, and I never let on.

posts.quote: THE SCHOOL PLAY / A BEDSHEET CURTAIN, A CARDBOARD CROWN, AND EVERY PARENT IN THE FRONT ROW
posts.caption: The school play was held in the gym, and the stage was a row of risers with a bedsheet curtain on a clothesline. Every shepherd wore a bathrobe and a dish towel held on with a necktie. The kid who got cast as the tree stood perfectly still and was somehow the hit of the evening. Someone forgot a line, someone waved at their mother, and nobody minded. The folding chairs were full, and the cookies on the card table were gone before the final bow. Every parent clapped like it was the main stage.
posts.first: My mother sewed my costume out of a bedspread and never let me forget it. She sat in the second row with a flashbulb camera she didn't know how to use. The one picture that came out is mostly her thumb.

posts.quote: THE BACK SEAT HAD AN INVISIBLE LINE DOWN THE MIDDLE, AND ONE ELBOW ACROSS IT STARTED A WAR.
posts.caption: Every back seat had a border, and nobody ever drew it down. It ran along the seam of the vinyl, and everyone knew exactly where it was. One elbow an inch over the line and the shouting began. Dad would look in the rearview mirror and say he'd turn this car around, though he never did. The miles went by, the arms stayed crossed, and the fields rolled past the windows. By the time you pulled into the driveway, the war was forgotten and somebody had fallen asleep.
posts.first: My brother and I fought over that line for eleven years. Dad finally put a folded blanket down the middle of the seat, and we fought over that too. I'd give a lot to be squeezed against that window again.
